title: A minor's chat and wellbeing data leaks through a contractor export

text: Monitoring alert: a debugging export of chat logs (412 student records, Grades 9-11, ages 14-17: names, class, planner entries and wellbeing check-in notes) was written to a publicly readable storage bucket by a contractor's script on Sunday night. Access logs show three downloads from unknown IP addresses.

rationale: Matched tags ['breach', 'minor_data'] to my mandate; actions are taken from my rule table and each is grounded in the best-matching excerpt from my sources.

actions.action: Contain the leak (revoke exposed links/tokens, rotate keys, preserve logs) and notify the UAE Data Office with the nature of the breach, DPO details, likely effects and corrective measures; then inform affected students and guardians.
Treat the records as children's data: restrict access to the minimum staff needed and stop any non-essential processing of them.

deadlines: PDPL Art. 9: 'within the period ... set by the Executive Regulations' (no number of hours in the law itself)

text: A guardian files a complaint with the UAE Data Office saying an AI study app leaked her daughter's personal data and nobody has told her what happened.
Forensics update: the bucket belongs to the model-logging vendor and is hosted outside the UAE. 37 of the 412 records came in through a school-connector licence; the rest are family accounts.

gaps.title: No statutory clock for notifying a breach of children's data
Education platforms may be exempted from the under-13 data rule by a resolution that does not exist yet
Teenagers' consent is not addressed by the PDPL
The same AI tutor falls under different data-protection regimes depending on who deploys it
Low-cost model access pushes student data across borders on terms schools cannot check
Several regulators can claim a children's-data AI incident; none is named lead
